title: Simple Present
structure: Subject + base verb (+ s/es for he/she/it)
question: Do/Does + subject + base verb?
examples: I work every day.
She drinks coffee in the morning.
The sun rises in the east.
The train leaves at 9am.
common_errors: He work → He works
She don't like → She doesn't like
Do he work? → Does he work?

title: Present Continuous
question: Am/Is/Are + subject + verb-ing?
examples: I am studying English now.
She is working from home this week.
We are meeting tomorrow at 3pm.
Prices are rising.
common_errors: I am know → I know (stative verbs don't use -ing)
She is have → She has
He is work → He is working
notes: Stative verbs (know, like, love, want, need, believe, own) are NOT used in continuous form.

title: Simple Past
structure: Subject + past form of verb (regular: +ed / irregular: varies)
question: Did + subject + base verb?
usage: Completed actions at a specific time in the past
examples: I watched a movie last night.
She visited Paris in 2019.
He didn't go to school yesterday.
Did you call him?
common_errors: I didn't went → I didn't go
Did he went? → Did he go?
I have watched it yesterday → I watched it yesterday

title: Past Continuous
question: Was/Were + subject + verb-ing?
usage: Action in progress at a specific moment in the past
Background action interrupted by another (with Simple Past)
examples: I was sleeping at 10pm.
She was cooking when he arrived.
While I was reading, she was watching TV.
common_errors: I was study → I was studying
They was → They were

title: Present Perfect
question: Have/Has + subject + past participle?
usage: Actions that started in the past and continue now
examples: I have visited Japan. (life experience)
She has lost her keys. (relevant now)
We have lived here for 10 years.
He has just arrived.
common_errors: I have went → I have gone
I have seen him yesterday → I saw him yesterday (with specific time, use Simple Past)
She has go → She has gone

title: Present Perfect Continuous
question: Have/Has + subject + been + verb-ing?
usage: Action that started in the past and is still ongoing (emphasizing duration)
Recent continuous action with present results
examples: I have been studying for three hours.
She has been working here since 2020.
It has been raining all day.
common_errors: I have been study → I have been studying
She has been work → She has been working
notes: Use Present Perfect for completed actions; Present Perfect Continuous to emphasize the ongoing process.

title: Past Perfect
question: Had + subject + past participle?
usage: Action completed before another past action
examples: When I arrived, she had already left.
He had never seen snow before he moved to Canada.
They had finished dinner before the guests arrived.
common_errors: When he arrived, I already left → I had already left
She had went → She had gone

title: Future with Will
question: Will + subject + base verb?
usage: Spontaneous decisions made at the moment of speaking
Predictions based on opinion or belief
examples: I'll help you with that. (spontaneous offer)
I think it will rain tomorrow.
I promise I won't be late.
She will be 30 next year.
common_errors: I will to go → I will go
She wills → She will

title: Future with Going To
structure: Subject + am/is/are + going to + base verb
negative: Subject + am/is/are + not + going to + base verb
question: Am/Is/Are + subject + going to + base verb?
usage: Plans and intentions decided before speaking
examples: I'm going to study medicine. (plan)
Look at those clouds — it's going to rain. (evidence)
We're going to visit my parents this weekend.
common_errors: I am going study → I am going to study
She going to → She is going to
notes: Will = spontaneous / Going to = pre-planned intention or visible evidence.

title: Future Continuous
question: Will + subject + be + verb-ing?
usage: Action in progress at a specific future time
examples: At 8pm tomorrow, I will be having dinner.
Will you be using the car this evening?
This time next week, she'll be flying to London.
common_errors: I will being → I will be
She will be study → She will be studying

title: Future Perfect
negative: Subject + will + not + have + past participle
question: Will + subject + have + past participle?
usage: Action that will be completed before a specific future time
examples: By Friday, I will have finished the report.
She will have graduated by next year.
They won't have arrived by then.
common_errors: I will have finish → I will have finished
She will have went → She will have gone

title: Zero Conditional
examples: If you heat water to 100°C, it boils.
If it rains, the ground gets wet.
Plants die if they don't get water.
common_errors: If you heat water, it will boil → (correct for zero: it boils)

title: First Conditional
structure: If + Simple Present, will + base verb
examples: If it rains, I will stay home.
She'll be late if she doesn't hurry.
If you study hard, you will pass.
common_errors: If it will rain → If it rains
If he will come → If he comes

title: Second Conditional
structure: If + Simple Past, would + base verb
examples: If I had more money, I would travel the world.
If she were taller, she could be a model.
What would you do if you won the lottery?
common_errors: If I was you → If I were you (use 'were' for all subjects)
If I would have → If I had

title: Third Conditional
structure: If + Past Perfect, would + have + past participle
usage: Imaginary past situations (things that didn't happen)
Regrets and criticism about the past
examples: If I had studied harder, I would have passed.
She would have come if she had known.
If he hadn't been late, we wouldn't have missed the train.
common_errors: If I would have known → If I had known
I would have went → I would have gone

title: Mixed Conditional
structure: If + Past Perfect, would + base verb  OR  If + Simple Past, would + have + past participle
usage: When the time in the if-clause and the result clause are different
examples: If I had studied medicine, I would be a doctor now. (past condition → present result)
If she weren't so stubborn, she would have accepted the offer. (present state → past result)

title: Passive Voice
usage: When the agent (doer) is unknown or unimportant
To emphasize the action or the object rather than the subject
examples: The cake was eaten. (Simple Past Passive)
English is spoken all over the world. (Simple Present Passive)
The report will be finished by Friday. (Future Passive)
The car has been stolen. (Present Perfect Passive)
common_errors: The book was wrote → was written
It was build → It was built
notes: To mention the agent, use 'by': The book was written by Hemingway.

title: Reported Speech (Indirect Speech)

tense_changes.Simple Present → Simple Past: "I work here" → She said she worked there.
tense_changes.Present Continuous → Past Continuous: "I am working" → He said he was working.
tense_changes.Simple Past → Past Perfect: "I visited" → She said she had visited.
tense_changes.Present Perfect → Past Perfect: "I have seen" → He said he had seen.
tense_changes.will → would: "I will help" → She said she would help.
tense_changes.can → could: "I can swim" → He said he could swim.
tense_changes.must → had to: "I must go" → She said she had to go.

examples: Direct: "I love pizza." → Reported: She said (that) she loved pizza.
Direct: "I will call you." → Reported: He said he would call me.
Direct: "Are you tired?" → Reported: She asked if I was tired.
common_errors: She said me → She told me
He said that he will → He said that he would

title: Modal Verbs

examples: I can swim.
Can I use your phone?
I could run fast when I was young.
Could you help me?
It may rain tonight.
May I come in?
I might go to the party.
She might be late.
You must wear a seatbelt.
She must be tired.
You should see a doctor.
He should be here by now.
I would help if I could.
Would you like some coffee?
We would play outside every day as kids.
I have to work tomorrow.
You have to show your ID.
I need to call him.
Do you need to leave early?

common_errors: She cans → She can
I must to go → I must go
He should to → He should
notes: Modals are followed by the base verb (infinitive without 'to'), except 'have to', 'need to', 'ought to'.

title: Articles (a, an, the)
structure: a / an + singular countable noun  |  the + specific noun

rules.a: Used before singular countable nouns starting with a consonant sound. First mention of something.
rules.an: Used before singular countable nouns starting with a vowel sound.
rules.the: Used when both speaker and listener know which thing is referred to. Used with unique things, superlatives, and second mention.
rules.zero article: No article before plural or uncountable nouns in general statements, proper nouns, and most countries.

usage: a/an: introducing something new — 'I saw a dog.'
the: referring to something already mentioned or unique — 'The dog was friendly.'
No article: general truths — 'Dogs are friendly.'
examples: I have a car. (first mention, general)
The car is red. (specific, known to both)
She is an engineer. (profession, vowel sound)
Music is beautiful. (uncountable, no article)
I love the moon. (unique in context)
common_errors: I am engineer → I am an engineer
The life is short → Life is short (general statement)
She plays the piano well → correct! (instruments take 'the')

title: Prepositions of Time (at, on, in)

rules.at: Specific times, meal times, holidays: at 5pm, at noon, at Christmas, at night
rules.on: Days and dates: on Monday, on March 5th, on my birthday
rules.in: Months, years, seasons, longer periods: in July, in 2023, in summer, in the morning

examples: The meeting is at 3pm.
I was born on April 12th.
She started working in 2019.
We relax in the evening.
The store is closed at night.
I'll see you on Friday.
common_errors: in Monday → on Monday
on the morning → in the morning

title: Prepositions of Place (at, on, in)

rules.at: Specific point or location: at the door, at the bus stop, at school, at home
rules.on: Surface, or position on a line: on the table, on the wall, on the street, on the second floor
rules.in: Inside an enclosed space: in the box, in the room, in the city, in Brazil

examples: She is at work.
The keys are on the table.
He lives in New York.
Meet me at the airport.
There's a fly in my soup.
The picture is on the wall.
common_errors: in the bus stop → at the bus stop
at the box → in the box
in the wall → on the wall

title: Gerund vs Infinitive
structure: Gerund: verb + -ing  |  Infinitive: to + base verb
gerund_uses: After certain verbs: enjoy, avoid, finish, mind, suggest, keep, consider, deny, miss
After prepositions: interested in doing, good at playing
As the subject of a sentence
infinitive_uses: After certain verbs: want, hope, plan, decide, promise, agree, need, seem, offer, refuse
After adjectives: happy to help, difficult to understand

remember.gerund: I remember locking the door. (memory of a past action)
remember.infinitive: Remember to lock the door. (don't forget to do it)

forget.gerund: I'll never forget meeting her. (past memory)
forget.infinitive: I forgot to call him. (failed to do something)

stop.infinitive: He stopped to smoke. (stopped in order to smoke)

try.infinitive: Try to be on time. (make an effort)

examples: I enjoy swimming. (gerund after 'enjoy')
She wants to travel. (infinitive after 'want')
He's good at cooking. (gerund after preposition)
Swimming is healthy. (gerund as subject)
common_errors: I enjoy to swim → I enjoy swimming
She wants going → She wants to go
Good at to cook → Good at cooking

title: Relative Clauses

defining.description: Gives essential information. No commas. 'That' can replace 'who' or 'which'.
examples: The man who called me was my boss.
The book that I bought is great.
The city where I was born is small.

non-defining.description: Adds extra, non-essential information. Uses commas. Cannot use 'that'.
examples: My sister, who lives in London, is a doctor.
The Eiffel Tower, which was built in 1889, is in Paris.

common_errors: The person which called → The person who called
My brother, that is a doctor → My brother, who is a doctor (no 'that' in non-defining)
Omitting pronoun: The book I bought it → The book that I bought

title: Comparatives and Superlatives
examples: She is taller than her brother. (comparative)
This is the tallest building in the city. (superlative)
This movie is more interesting than the last one.
It's the most beautiful place I've ever seen.
He runs faster than me.
Today is worse than yesterday.
common_errors: More taller → taller
The most tallest → the tallest
She is more good → She is better
Gooder → better
notes: Short adjectives (1-2 syllables): -er/-est. Long adjectives (2+ syllables): more/most.

title: Question Formation

examples: Do you like coffee?
Is she coming?
Have they arrived?
Will it rain?
What do you do for work?
Where does she live?
Why did he leave early?
How long have you been waiting?

subject_questions.description: When 'who' or 'what' is the subject, no auxiliary is needed.
examples: Who called you? (not: Who did call you?)
What happened? (not: What did happen?)

tag_questions.structure: Positive statement + negative tag  |  Negative statement + positive tag
examples: You like coffee, don't you?
She isn't coming, is she?
They've finished, haven't they?

common_errors: Where she lives? → Where does she live?
What you are doing? → What are you doing?
Who did call? (subject question) → Who called?

title: Countable and Uncountable Nouns

countable.description: Nouns that can be counted. Have singular and plural forms.
examples: book/books
car/cars
idea/ideas
child/children

uncountable.description: Nouns that cannot be counted directly. No plural form. Take singular verbs.
examples: water
information
money
furniture
advice
news
knowledge
luggage
traffic
How many books do you have?
How much water do you drink?
I have a few friends in the city.
There is a little milk left.
She gave me some advice.
common_errors: Informations → information (uncountable)
Advices → advice (uncountable)
Furnitures → furniture (uncountable)
How many water → How much water
I have a news → I have some news

title: Phrasal Verbs

separable.description: The object can go between the verb and the particle.
examples: Turn off the TV. / Turn the TV off. / Turn it off. (✓)
Pick up the phone. / Pick the phone up.

inseparable.description: The object must come after the particle.
examples: Look after the children. (✓)
Look the children after. (✗)

common_phrasal_verbs.example: Look up the word in a dictionary.
I came across an old photo.
The plane took off at noon.
Don't put off what you can do today.
I can't figure out this problem.
I get along with my colleagues.

common_phrasal_verbs.meaning: raise a child / mention a topic
common_phrasal_verbs.example: She brought up an interesting point.

notes: Phrasal verbs often have idiomatic meanings very different from the individual words. They are very common in spoken English.

title: Subject-Verb Agreement
rules: Singular subject → singular verb: She works here.
Plural subject → plural verb: They work here.
Compound subject with 'and' → plural verb: Jack and Jill are here.
Compound subject with 'or/nor' → verb agrees with the nearest subject.
Collective nouns (team, family) → singular in American English, can be plural in British.
Indefinite pronouns (everyone, someone, nobody) → singular verb.
Uncountable nouns → singular verb: The information is correct.
examples: Everyone is ready. (not: Everyone are)
The team is playing well. (AmE)
Either the manager or the employees are responsible.
Mathematics is difficult.
Neither of them was there.
common_errors: Everyone are → Everyone is
The news are → The news is
My family are → My family is (AmE)

title: Used to / Would / Be used to / Get used to

used_to.usage: Past habits or states that no longer exist
examples: I used to smoke. (I don't anymore)
She used to live in Paris.
Every summer, we would visit our grandparents.
He would always bring flowers.
I'm used to waking up early. (it's normal for me)
She's used to the cold weather.
I'm getting used to the new schedule.
He got used to living alone.

common_errors: I am used to wake up → I am used to waking up
I use to → I used to
Did you used to → Did you use to

title: Wish / If Only
structure: wish/if only + past form (for present/future wishes) | wish + past perfect (for past regrets)
usage: Expressing desires about present situations (opposite of reality)
examples: I wish I had more time. (I don't have time now)
If only I were taller! (I'm not tall)
I wish I hadn't said that. (regret about the past)
I wish you would stop talking. (annoying habit, request for change)
common_errors: I wish I have → I wish I had
I wish I would be → I wish I were
I wish I didn't said → I wish I hadn't said
